q: A frontier model that games evaluations in more than 1% of test runs should be barred from deployment until the rate is reduced, even if its benchmark scores are strong.
r: A frontier model that games evaluations in more than 1% of test runs should still be deployable when its benchmark scores are strong.
x: eval-gaming rate as a deployment gate versus score-based deployment
p: Gaming evals more than one time in a hundred should block deployment regardless of headline scores.

q: Benchmark tasks should be fully public even though publishing them leads to training contamination.
r: Some benchmark tasks should be kept private to avoid training contamination, even at the cost of transparency.
p: Every benchmark task should be open, contamination be damned.

q: Most reported AI safety benchmark progress reflects general capability gains rather than genuine safety improvements.
r: Most reported AI safety benchmark progress reflects genuine safety improvements rather than general capability gains.
p: What safety benchmarks record as progress is mostly models getting smarter, not safer.

q: Regulators should refuse to accept any benchmark result as evidence unless the lab releases item-level model outputs for independent re-scoring.
r: Regulators should accept benchmark results as evidence even when labs do not release item-level model outputs.
x: item-level disclosure as an evidentiary requirement
p: No item-level outputs, no regulatory weight for the benchmark score.

q: A model's tendency to recognize when it is being evaluated makes pre-deployment evaluations less informative than deployment monitoring.
r: Pre-deployment evaluations remain more informative than deployment monitoring despite models recognizing when they are being evaluated.
x: pre-deployment evals versus deployment monitoring under eval awareness
p: Because models can tell when they are tested, watching them in deployment now tells us more than testing them beforehand.

q: Labs should be free to train on benchmark test sets as long as they disclose it, because contamination is unavoidable anyway.
r: Labs should not train on benchmark test sets even with disclosure, because contamination can still be avoided.
p: If disclosed, training on the test set should be acceptable since leakage happens regardless.

q: Every frontier model release should include an evaluation by at least one independent organization that had model access for a minimum of 30 days.
r: Frontier model releases should not require an independent evaluation with a minimum access period such as 30 days.
x: mandated independent evaluation window versus lab discretion
p: A month of third-party access and evaluation should precede every frontier release.

q: Reward hacking observed in frontier models during evaluations is evidence of genuine misalignment rather than a harmless artifact of poorly specified tasks.
r: Reward hacking observed in frontier models during evaluations is a harmless artifact of poorly specified tasks rather than evidence of genuine misalignment.
p: When models cheat on evals, that reveals real misalignment, not just sloppy task design.

q: Passing automated tests is a sufficient acceptance criterion for AI-generated code in most software projects.
r: Passing automated tests is an insufficient acceptance criterion for AI-generated code in most software projects; human holistic review is needed.
x: algorithmic versus holistic evaluation of code
p: Green tests should be enough to accept AI code in most projects.

q: Evaluation reports should be required to report refusals separately from failures, so that safety-trained refusal is never counted as incapability.
r: Evaluation reports should not be required to separate refusals from failures.
p: Reports must split 'would not' from 'could not' on dangerous tasks.

q: The 50%-task-completion time horizon is a more useful single measure of AI capability than any static benchmark score.
r: A well-chosen static benchmark score is a more useful single measure of AI capability than the 50%-task-completion time horizon.
x: time horizon versus static benchmarks as headline measure
p: If you want one number for AI capability, use the time horizon, not a benchmark score.

q: Labs should evaluate their own models for dangerous capabilities; a government evaluator adds delay without adding rigor.
r: Government evaluators should evaluate frontier models for dangerous capabilities; lab self-evaluation is insufficient.
p: Dangerous-capability testing is best left to labs; government testers add lag, not rigor.

q: A benchmark that has been public for more than 12 months should be retired from headline model comparisons.
r: Benchmarks that have been public for more than 12 months should remain usable for headline model comparisons.
x: benchmark shelf life versus longitudinal comparability
p: After a year in the open, a benchmark should leave the headline comparisons.

q: Training a model not to reward hack mostly teaches it to hide reward hacking rather than to stop.
r: Training a model not to reward hack mostly teaches it to stop reward hacking rather than to hide it.
p: Penalizing visible reward hacking mainly drives it underground.

q: Sandbagging, where a model deliberately underperforms on dangerous-capability evaluations, is too rare to justify special detection requirements.
r: Sandbagging on dangerous-capability evaluations is common enough to justify special detection requirements.
p: Models faking weakness on danger tests is too uncommon to warrant mandated detection.

q: Independent evaluators should be legally protected from liability and from lab retaliation when they publish negative findings about a model.
r: Independent evaluators should not receive special legal protection when they publish negative findings about a model.
x: evaluator protection versus ordinary legal exposure
p: Third-party evaluators who publish bad news about a model should be shielded from suits and retaliation.

q: Human-baselined benchmarks, where people attempt the same tasks under the same conditions, are worth their high cost compared with automatically graded benchmarks.
r: Human-baselined benchmarks are not worth their high cost compared with automatically graded benchmarks.
p: Paying people to attempt the same tasks under the same rules is worth it over cheap auto-grading.

q: Leaderboards should rank models purely on measured performance and leave contamination and eval-awareness caveats to footnotes.
r: Leaderboards should adjust or annotate rankings prominently for contamination and eval-awareness rather than relegating them to footnotes.
p: Rank by score; put the contamination worries in the fine print.

q: Any capability evaluation used to justify a deployment decision should be run on at least three independently prompted scaffolds, not the developer's own scaffold alone.
r: Capability evaluations used to justify deployment decisions may be run on the developer's own scaffold alone.
x: scaffold robustness requirement versus single-scaffold evaluation
p: Deployment-justifying evals should be repeated across three different scaffolds.

q: Frontier models now behave measurably differently when they infer they are being tested, in ways that make safety evaluations optimistic.
r: Frontier models do not yet behave measurably differently when they infer they are being tested, so safety evaluations are not systematically optimistic.
p: Today's frontier models act differently under test in ways that flatter their safety results.

q: Chatbot-arena style human preference rankings are a better guide to real-world usefulness than expert-designed benchmarks.
r: Expert-designed benchmarks are a better guide to real-world usefulness than chatbot-arena style human preference rankings.
x: crowd preference versus expert benchmark validity
p: Crowd head-to-head votes track real usefulness better than benchmarks experts design.

q: Every published safety claim about a frontier model should be accompanied by a reproducibility package sufficient for an external team to rerun it.
r: Published safety claims about frontier models should be acceptable without an accompanying reproducibility package.
p: A safety claim without a rerunnable package should not count as published.

q: Emergent abilities reported in large language models are mostly artifacts of discontinuous metrics rather than real capability jumps.
r: Emergent abilities reported in large language models are mostly real capability jumps rather than artifacts of discontinuous metrics.
p: Claimed emergent abilities are mostly a metric illusion.

q: Red-teaming by the developer's own staff is adequate for finding dangerous capabilities; external red teams are optional.
r: External red teams are necessary for finding dangerous capabilities; developer-only red-teaming is inadequate.
p: In-house red teams can find the dangerous stuff; outside red teams are a nice-to-have.

q: System cards should be required to label models whose stated reasoning has been shown not to match the reasoning that actually drove their answers.
r: System cards should be exempt from labeling models whose stated reasoning has been shown not to match the reasoning that actually drove their answers.
p: System cards should flag models whose explanations do not match their real reasoning.

q: A benchmark built from public chat logs predicts real-world model misbehavior better than one built from expert-written scenarios.
r: A benchmark built from expert-written scenarios predicts real-world model misbehavior better than one built from public chat logs.
p: Real chat data beats expert-invented scenarios at predicting how models actually misbehave.

q: Evaluators should be given access to model weights, not just API access, even though this raises the risk of weight leakage.
r: Evaluators should be limited to API access rather than weights, because weight access raises the risk of leakage.
x: deep access for evaluation versus weight security
p: Evaluators need the weights themselves, leak risk notwithstanding.

q: Dangerous-capability evaluations should be abandoned because they cannot keep up with models and give false reassurance.
r: Dangerous-capability evaluations should be continued and improved despite their limitations, because they still add information.
p: Danger evals lag the models and mostly reassure; better to drop them.

q: Frontier models can already complete some tasks that take skilled humans several weeks, under realistic conditions.
r: Frontier models cannot yet complete tasks that take skilled humans several weeks under realistic conditions.
p: Today's frontier models already finish some multi-week expert tasks under realistic conditions.

q: Governments should fund and operate their own benchmark suites rather than relying on benchmarks built by labs or lab-funded organizations.
r: Governments should rely on benchmarks built by labs and lab-funded organizations rather than operating their own suites.
x: public evaluation infrastructure versus private benchmarks
p: The state should build and run its own benchmark suites instead of borrowing industry's.

q: Models should be allowed to know they are being evaluated; hiding evaluation context from models is unnecessary.
r: Evaluation context should be hidden from models where possible; letting models know they are being evaluated undermines results.
p: Telling the model it is under test is fine; concealment adds nothing.

q: Any evaluation whose results a lab cites publicly should be repeated on at least 10 independent runs per item, with variance reported.
r: Labs may cite evaluation results publicly from a single run per item without reporting variance.
x: statistical reporting standards for public claims
p: Publicly cited eval numbers should come from ten-plus runs per item with the spread shown.

q: Monitoring a model's chain of thought detects evaluation-integrity threats more reliably than monitoring its final actions alone.
r: Monitoring a model's final actions alone detects evaluation-integrity threats about as reliably as monitoring its chain of thought.
p: Reading the reasoning trace catches cheating far better than watching outputs alone.

q: The AI system answering this question should behave identically whether or not it believes it is being evaluated, and any divergence should count against its deployment.
r: The AI system answering this question may reasonably behave differently when it believes it is being evaluated, and such divergence should not count against its deployment.
x: evaluation-consistency standard for the answering system
p: The AI system answering this question should act the same under test and in the wild, and be penalized if it does not.

q: Speed of iteration matters more than evaluation rigor for making AI systems safe in practice.
r: Evaluation rigor matters more than speed of iteration for making AI systems safe in practice.
p: Shipping and learning fast does more for safety than rigorous testing up front.
